prompt: What does creating the `SparkSession` do?
hint: It is the program's connection to the cluster.

choices.text: Reads the input files into memory
choices.why: Nothing is read until an action asks for a result.

choices.text: Connects the driver to the cluster and gets executors
choices.why: Right. Everything after it goes through it.

choices.text: Starts the master and the workers if they are down
choices.why: Those are started by `start-master.sh` and `start-worker.sh`.

choices.text: Compiles the Python program to Java
choices.why: Python stays Python; the driver talks to its Java half.

prompt: Match each piece of a PySpark program to where it runs.

pairs.right: A Python process beside each executor

prompt: Why can a notebook left open overnight slow other people's jobs?
hint: What does an open session hold?

choices.text: It locks the files it has read
choices.why: Reading locks nothing.

choices.text: Its session keeps its executors
choices.why: Right. Its share of the cluster stays taken.

choices.text: The driver uploads the notebook to every worker
choices.why: Nothing like that happens.

choices.text: Notebooks rerun every cell every hour to keep the results fresh
choices.why: They run a cell when you run it.

prompt: What does Spark keep for an RDD, so that a lost partition can be rebuilt?

choices.text: A snapshot written to HDFS after each step
choices.why: That is MapReduce's way; Spark avoids it.

choices.text: Nothing; a lost partition fails the job
choices.why: Lesson 2's job survived a lost executor.

choices.text: A copy of every partition on another executor
choices.why: Partitions are not stored by default; the recipe is kept.

choices.text: Its lineage
choices.why: Right. The recipe, from the files to the result.

prompt: Why did `textFile` make 365 partitions, one per file, rather than splitting the larger files?
hint: Can you start reading a gzip file in the middle?

choices.text: Spark makes one partition per file whatever the format
choices.why: A large uncompressed file is split into many, as lesson 3's ten blocks were.

choices.text: The `day=` directories forbid splitting
choices.why: Directories have nothing to do with it.

choices.text: There are 365 executors
choices.why: There are three.

choices.text: A gzip file cannot be split; one task reads it whole
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10 meets formats that can be split.

prompt: In the lineage, the RDD that marks the boundary between the map side and the reduce side is called ___RDD.
Which of these are actions, that start a job? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `filter(...)`
choices.why: A transformation: it only adds a step.

choices.text: `groupBy(...)`
choices.why: A transformation too, however much work it will cause later.

choices.text: `count()`
choices.why: Yes. It needs a number.

choices.text: `show()`
choices.why: Yes. It needs rows to print.

choices.text: `write.parquet(...)`
choices.why: Yes. Writing needs every row.

prompt: `views.count()` ran twice. Why did the second call read every file again?
hint: Is `views` a result or a recipe?

choices.text: The first count failed silently and had to be redone
choices.why: Both printed the same correct number.

choices.text: The second count had a different filter
choices.why: Same `views`, same filter.

choices.text: Spark rereads files whenever an hour has passed
choices.why: No such rule.

choices.text: `views` is a recipe; nothing was kept
choices.why: Right. Two actions, two jobs, unless you ask to keep the data (lesson 9).

prompt: What does laziness let Spark do that running each line at once would not?
hint: When does Spark see the whole program?

choices.text: Skip actions the programmer did not mean
choices.why: Every action runs.

choices.text: See all the steps before running any
choices.why: Right. It can fuse steps and read only what is needed.

choices.text: Avoid the shuffle in every grouping
choices.why: A grouping still needs its shuffle.

choices.text: Use less disk for the input files
choices.why: The input files are what they are.

prompt: Read with only `header`, every column of the CSV came out as a string except `day`. Why `day`?

choices.text: Spark always reads the last column as a date
choices.why: No such rule.

choices.text: It is the only column with a header
choices.why: Every column has a header name; none of the file's columns has a type.

choices.text: It comes from the directory names
choices.why: Right. Partition values are typed by Spark itself.

choices.text: The generator wrote it as a date in the file
choices.why: It is not in the files at all.

prompt: Why can Spark optimise `where(F.col('kind') == 'purchase')` but not `filter(lambda line: ',purchase,' in line)`?

choices.text: A column expression is readable; a lambda is opaque
choices.why: Right. Spark can reorder and push down what it can read.

choices.text: The lambda reads a different file
choices.why: Same data either way.

choices.text: `where` is run on the driver
choices.why: It runs on the executors, like everything else.

choices.text: Lambdas are forbidden on DataFrames
choices.why: They are allowed as UDFs, at a cost.

prompt: What did `inferSchema` cost in `schema.py`?
hint: What does Spark have to do to guess?

choices.text: Nothing; the guess comes from the header line
choices.why: The header has names, not types.

choices.text: Extra memory on the driver only
choices.why: The cost is time, a whole extra pass over the data.

choices.text: A full read of the input before the real job
choices.why: Right. Tens of seconds on 1.3 GB, every time.

choices.text: A read of the first ten rows
choices.why: By default it reads everything.

prompt: The guess made `event_id` an `integer` and the declaration made it `LONG`. Which is right, and why?
hint: What happens when the id passes about 2.1 billion?

choices.text: `integer`, because the data says so
choices.why: This year's data says so. Next year's may not.

choices.text: Either; Spark converts automatically on overflow
choices.why: It does not widen a column by itself.

choices.text: `LONG`: the id will outgrow an `int`
choices.why: Right. A guess only knows the data it saw.

choices.text: `integer`: it is smaller and therefore faster
choices.why: A wrong type is not a saving.

prompt: With a declared schema, `.option("mode", "___")` stops the job at the first row that does not fit.
Why was the Python UDF slower than the built-in `hour`?

choices.text: Python's datetime gives a different hour
choices.why: Both gave the same 24 hours.

choices.text: Every row travels to a Python process and back
choices.why: Right. Serialise, send, call, send back, 24 million times.

choices.text: The UDF read the files twice
choices.why: Each run read them once.

choices.text: UDFs run on the driver
choices.why: They run beside the executors.

prompt: Order the options for computing something Spark has no function for, from first to try to last.
hint: Built-ins first; one row at a time last.

prompt: Besides time, what does a UDF cost the query?

choices.text: It cannot be used inside `groupBy`
choices.why: `udf.py` grouped by one.

choices.text: It doubles the size of the output
choices.why: The output is the same.

choices.text: The planner is blind to what it does
choices.why: Right. Lesson 6 shows a pushed-down filter lost to a UDF.

choices.text: It forces the data into one partition
choices.why: Partitions are unchanged.

prompt: What does `to_parquet.py` add to the data that the raw CSV did not carry?
hint: What did every reader have to supply before?

choices.text: The types, stored in the files
choices.why: Right. A reader gets `ts` as a timestamp for free.

choices.text: New events from the website
choices.why: Same 24 million events.

choices.text: A smaller size on disk
choices.why: Here it came out larger, 396 MB against 243.

choices.text: A partition for every visitor instead of every day
choices.why: Still one per day.

prompt: Match each write mode to what it does when the output already exists.
hint: One of them is the default.

pairs.right: Adds files beside the old ones

prompt: A nightly job writes with `mode("append")` and is run twice by mistake. What happens?

choices.text: The second run fails because the files exist
choices.why: That is `error` mode, not `append`.

choices.text: That day's data is doubled, with no error
choices.why: Right. Lesson 11's table formats are one cure.

choices.text: Spark notices the duplicate rows and skips them
choices.why: Append checks nothing.

choices.text: The first run's files are replaced
choices.why: That is `overwrite`.

prompt: In `spark-sql`, what does ``parquet.`data/silver/books` `` mean?

choices.text: A table called `books` in a database called `parquet`
choices.why: There is no such database; `parquet` names the format.

choices.text: The Parquet files at that path, used as a table
choices.why: Right. A way to query files where a table name would go.

choices.text: A view created by `to_parquet.py`
choices.why: Views live only inside the program that made them.

choices.text: A command to convert the books to Parquet
choices.why: It only reads.

prompt: How long does a view made with `createOrReplaceTempView` last?

choices.text: As long as the session
choices.why: Right. Names that outlive programs need a catalogue (lesson 12).

choices.text: One query
choices.why: Any number of queries in the same session can use it.

choices.text: Until the cluster is restarted
choices.why: It dies with the program, long before.

choices.text: Forever, in `spark-warehouse`
choices.why: Nothing is written for a temporary view.

prompt: Why did the DataFrame and the SQL versions take the same time?

choices.text: Both happen to be short
choices.why: Length of code does not decide speed.

choices.text: SQL is translated into the RDD version
choices.why: The RDD version was slower; SQL is not that.

choices.text: The second one reused the first one's result
choices.why: Nothing was cached; each read the files.

choices.text: They compile to the same plan
choices.why: Right. Two spellings, one planner, one plan.

prompt: Why was the RDD version the slowest of the three?
hint: What are its filter and map made of?

choices.text: It read Parquet instead of CSV
choices.why: It read the same CSV files.

choices.text: It counted a different thing
choices.why: All three answers were identical.

choices.text: Its functions are Python, and every line goes to Python and back
choices.why: Right. And to an RDD a line is a string, so no column can be skipped.

choices.text: RDDs cannot use more than one executor
choices.why: It ran on all three.

prompt: Match each situation to the API the lesson suggests.
hint: Table-shaped questions do not need RDDs.

pairs.left: A report query read by analysts who know SQL
A pipeline whose columns are chosen at runtime
Records with no table shape at all

prompt: A program reads the clicks, filters purchases, then calls `count()`, `show()` and `write.parquet()` on the result. How many times are the files read?

choices.text: Four, counting the filter
choices.why: The filter is a transformation and reads nothing itself.

choices.text: Three, one per action
choices.why: Right. Each action is a job, and nothing is kept between them.

choices.text: Once, because Spark caches what it read
choices.why: Not unless you ask, which is lesson 9.

choices.text: Once, when the files are opened
choices.why: Opening reads nothing; each action reads everything.

prompt: A job reads CSV with `inferSchema` and computes a weekday with a Python UDF. Which change saves the most, and why?

choices.text: Nothing; both costs are fixed
choices.why: Both are avoidable and both scale with the data.

choices.text: Both: a declared schema and the built-in `dayofweek`
choices.why: Right. One removes a whole extra read, the other the trip to Python per row.

choices.text: More executors and memory, keeping every line of the code as it is
choices.why: Both costs grow with the data, and more executors only spread them.

choices.text: Rewriting the job with RDDs
choices.why: That keeps the Python per row and loses the planner.
